cards.title: The Halden Chronometer
cards.briefing:
At **09:10 on Tuesday**, conservator Ines Duarte opened the display case in Gallery 3 of the Saltmarsh Bay Maritime Museum to dust the museum's treasure: the brass **Halden chronometer** that once kept time on a whaling ship. It was not the Halden chronometer. Someone had swapped it for a copy.

The museum was open on Sunday, closed all day Monday, and the display key never leaves the electronic key box in the curator's office. Nothing is broken and no alarm went off.

The museum board wants answers before the police arrive: **who** made the swap, **when**, **whose badge** opened the key box, **how** the real chronometer left the building, and **where** it is now.

evidence.title: Condition report, Gallery 3
evidence.content:
**Saltmarsh Bay Maritime Museum — condition check**

**Saturday, 17:30** (I. Duarte): Halden chronometer, Gallery 3. Serial plate reads **No. 1847**. Ticking normally. Case locked, display key D3 returned to the key box.

**Tuesday, 09:10** (I. Duarte): Object in the case is NOT the original. Serial plate reads **No. 1874**. It does not tick.

*Note:* the volunteers' touch-table copy in the Education Room was deliberately stamped **No. 1874** so the two could never be confused. The Education Room touch table is empty this morning.

evidence.title: Interview: Nina Osei (night guard)
evidence.content:
**Q:** What were your hours on Monday?

**Nina:** Eight in the evening to six in the morning. The museum is closed on Mondays, so it's quiet.

**Q:** Did you see anyone?

**Nina:** Not inside. I was at the front desk doing the weekly paperwork from about nine to ten. Around half past nine I went to the window of the staff kitchen to make tea, and I saw Dr Lindqvist's car in the staff car park — the green estate with the anchor sticker — backed right up to the loading dock with its boot open. I thought she was working late again, so I didn't go out.

**Q:** Did you hear the loading dock door?

**Nina:** No. From the front desk you hear nothing back there.

evidence.title: Security company note on the camera footage
evidence.content:
**Harbourside Security — footage review**

The museum has one camera, covering the main entrance and the front desk. There are no cameras at the back of the building.

Monday: the guard (N. Osei) is visible at the front desk **without a break from 20:55 to 22:10**. Nobody used the main entrance between Sunday 17:05 and Tuesday 08:50.

evidence.title: Interview: Felix Marsh (volunteer guide)
evidence.content:
**Q:** You made the touch-table copy of the chronometer?

**Felix:** Last winter, yes. I build ship models. I stamped it 1874 on purpose, so nobody could pass it off as the real thing.

**Q:** Where were you on Monday evening?

**Felix:** Playing the cello with the Saltmarsh Community Orchestra at the Town Hall, half past seven to ten. Half the town was there.

**Q:** Your volunteer badge is VOL-07?

**Felix:** It was. I lost it on Sunday afternoon — I think I left it on a table in the museum café around four. I emailed the office on Sunday evening to ask for a new one and haven't heard back.

evidence.title: Interview: Dr Ruth Lindqvist (curator)
evidence.content:
**Q:** Where were you on Monday evening?

**Ruth:** The museum was closed, so I left at six and spent the evening at home on Gull Terrace. I didn't go out again.

**Q:** Did you know Felix Marsh had lost his badge?

**Ruth:** No, this is the first I've heard of it. Volunteer badges are the office's business, not mine.

**Q:** Has anyone shown an interest in buying the chronometer?

**Ruth:** Collectors ask now and then. The board would never sell it, and I would never suggest it.

cards.walkthrough:
**The copy.** On Saturday the real chronometer (No. 1847) was checked and locked away (`condition-report`). On Tuesday the case held the volunteers' touch-table copy, stamped No. 1874 (`replica-plate`), and the Education Room table was empty. Someone had to open the case between Saturday 17:34 and Tuesday morning.

**When.** The display key D3 left the key box only once after Saturday: **Monday 21:12 to 21:41**, with the loading dock door opening at 21:38 (`building-log`). Nobody used the main entrance from Sunday's closing until Tuesday (`cctv-note`), so the swap happened on Monday night.

**Whose badge.** The key was taken with badge **VOL-07**, Felix Marsh's — but Felix says he lost it on Sunday (`felix-interview`), and at 21:20 on Monday he was on stage at the Town Hall (`concert-photo`). The guard, Nina, was on camera at the front desk the whole time (`cctv-note`). So someone else had Felix's badge.

**Who.** The café's lost-property book shows the badge was handed to **R. Lindqvist (curator)** on Sunday at 16:45 and signed for (`lost-property`). Ruth says she never knew the badge was lost and was at home all evening (`ruth-interview`), but at 21:30 Nina saw her green estate backed up to the loading dock with its boot open (`nina-interview`). The curator lied twice.

**How it left.** The loading dock is next to Gallery 3 and out of the camera's view (`floor-plan`). It opened at 21:38 (`building-log`), while Ruth's car waited outside with the boot open (`nina-interview`).

**Where it is now.** Three minutes after leaving, Ruth called Bay Couriers and then a dealer in Rotterdam (`ruth-phone`). The booking, made at 21:51, sent a 4 kg antique brass instrument from her home on Gull Terrace to **Kessler Fine Instruments, Rotterdam**, cash on delivery for EUR 38,000 (`courier-booking`). It was collected on Tuesday at 07:02 and is in transit with Bay Couriers.

**Why.** Ruth sold the museum's treasure to a private dealer and framed the volunteer who had made the copy.
